cues.text: The Rise of Iconoclasm
In 726, Byzantine Emperor Leo III began moving against the veneration of religious images (icons).

He was convinced — amid military setbacks against the advancing Muslim armies and possibly influenced by Jewish and Islamic aniconism — that image veneration bordered on idolatry and had drawn down divine punishment on the empire.
His son Constantine V pressed the policy further, convening a council at Hieria in 754 that condemned icons outright, styling itself (falsely, in the Church's later judgment) an ecumenical council.
The following decades saw widespread destruction of icons and mosaics, and the persecution — sometimes violent — of monks and clergy who defended their veneration.
Chief among them was St. John Damascene , writing safely from Muslim-ruled territory beyond Byzantine reach.
He argued that venerating an image of Christ was not idolatry but a fitting consequence of the Incarnation itself: God had truly taken a visible, depictable human form.
Empress Irene's Council
The tide turned when Empress Irene , acting as regent for her young son Constantine VI , moved to restore icon veneration after the death of her iconoclast husband, Leo IV.
She appointed a new patriarch, Tarasius , sympathetic to icons, and, with Pope Adrian I 's support, summoned a new ecumenical council.
A first attempt to open the council at Constantinople in 786 was broken up by iconoclast soldiers loyal to the memory of Constantine V. Irene replaced the mutinous garrison.
The following year, she reconvened the council at the safer location of Nicaea .
It was the same city that had hosted the first ecumenical council 462 years earlier.
The council opened on September 24, 787 with roughly 350 bishops and representatives present, including two legates of Pope Adrian I, and was presided over in practice by Patriarch Tarasius.
Vindicating the Icons

Over eight sessions the council examined Scripture and the writings of the Church Fathers on the making and honoring of images, and heard the retraction of several bishops who had supported the iconoclast council of 754.
The Fathers concluded that images of Christ, the Virgin, the angels, and the saints may rightly be venerated with a relative honor — proskynesis .
This honor passes to the person represented, while adoration ( latria ) in the full sense belongs to God alone.
The council's decree drew a careful distinction its critics did not always observe.
Honor shown to an icon is not the same as worship owed to God.
Rather, it resembles respect given to the Gospel book, the Cross, or holy relics—an extension of reverence, not a transfer of divinity into the object itself.
A Troubled Reception in the West
The council's reception outside the Greek East was complicated by a poor Latin translation of its acts.
It rendered the careful Greek distinction between proskynesis and latria in language that appeared to command the same worship for icons as for God.

On the strength of this flawed text, Frankish theologians under Charlemagne produced the Libri Carolini , a lengthy critique rejecting what they took the council to be teaching, and a Frankish council at Frankfurt in 794 formally repudiated it.

The confusion was eventually cleared up as accurate translations circulated and Rome's own acceptance of the council became clear, though the episode illustrates how easily a genuine council's teaching could be distorted by translation before it reached the wider Church.
Legacy

Nicaea II is counted as the seventh and last of the ecumenical councils recognized by both the Catholic Church and the Eastern Orthodox Church in full communion with one another before the later schism between East and West.

Iconoclasm flared up again in Byzantium in the early ninth century before being finally and permanently defeated in 843, an event still celebrated in the Byzantine liturgical calendar as the Feast of Orthodoxy .
The council's theological reasoning holds that honoring an image is not idolatry.
Instead, it is a legitimate consequence of God having taken visible, human form in Christ.
This reasoning remains the foundation of Catholic and Orthodox practice regarding sacred art, from icons and crucifixes to statues of the saints, to this day.
